from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(reader.pages))
out = Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
texts = []
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages, 1):
    txt = page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    texts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+txt)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a practical image-stitching problem with a modular, training-free approach: repair misaligned patches along an existing seam using dense correspondence and constrained local seam cutting.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, Baseline+LPAM improves SEAGULL seam SSIM from 0.638 to 0.696 and PSNR from 26.20 to 28.31.

The pipeline illustrations explain the approach clearly, and Figures 1, 5, and 6 provide useful visual evidence of repaired structural discontinuities. Preserving boundary labels when recomputing local seams is a sensible design choice.

The manuscript attributes its principal components and benchmark datasets, provides a code/dataset link, and reports implementation hardware. Its explicit discussion and illustration of failure cases help establish practical limitations.
weaknesses: The central flow modification is not specified consistently. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (5) defines f on a normalized spatial coordinate. The apparent intended operation—spatially weighting the original flow—is never explicitly formulated. Moreover, the sigmoid does not attain the claimed endpoint values, and continuity around the entire rectangular patch is not established. These ambiguities affect reproducibility; patch padding, overlapping-patch handling, and SIFT-flow settings also need clarification.

The incremental contribution over related seam-guided alignment methods is insufficiently established. Section II describes SEAGULL [25] as adapting alignment and [21] as using dense matching to estimate a smooth warp, then broadly characterizes prior methods as operating on settled alignments. Direct comparisons with Parallax and SEAGULL are limited to one visual example, and the particularly relevant dense-matching method [21] is not evaluated. Stronger differentiation and controlled comparisons are needed to establish the value of this particular repair strategy.

The evaluation supports improved local image agreement more strongly than improved overall perceptual quality. The seam metrics compare patches from the aligned images around the selected seam, and SSIM also drives patch selection. Such measurements do not adequately assess geometric distortion, object integrity, or artifacts introduced at patch boundaries. Dataset-level failure rates and an independent assessment of mosaic quality would strengthen the visual examples.

There are no quantitative component ablations establishing the contributions of SSIM/Otsu patch selection, spatial flow attenuation, and constrained seam merging. Figure 3 provides a useful qualitative comparison of sigmoid settings, but sensitivity to k, beta, and patch extent remains unmeasured.

The operating assumptions substantially restrict the advertised large-parallax applicability. The rule max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts uniformly poor seams, while small extracted patches can produce new discontinuities, as Figure 7 acknowledges. The discussion is valuable, but the frequency and severity of these failures are unquantified. The earlier assertion that false-positive patch selection cannot worsen results is therefore unsupported.

The efficiency advantage is not demonstrated against competing alignment-repair approaches. Table III reports roughly 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, often exceeding the original seam-cutting cost, while excluding initial alignment. Comparable end-to-end timings and image resolutions are needed to substantiate the efficiency claim.
